This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
- Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
The state judge is ordering Tennessee officials
to preserve evidence connected to the failed attempt
at executing Christa Pike by lethal injection a week ago.
On September 30th, Pike was to become the first woman
executed in Tennessee in nearly 200 years,
but she survived.
Today, Pike's attorney said their client woke up this week
in the hospital, angry and confused.
Tony Gonzalez of conversation WPLN
has more on today's court hearing.
- Nashville judge Aisha Miles ordered prison officials
to preserve medical supplies, remnants of the drug
pentobarbital, and communications about their decision-making
on the night of Christa Pike's scheduled execution.
After Pike's legal team argued she deserves visitation
similar to her time in prison, Miles also granted them
more access to her in the hospital.
- The same protocols that would have been followed
while she is incarcerated at the women's prison
should be followed there.
- Pike was unconscious for more than five days
following the botched execution,
but her attorneys say she is now able to speak.
For NPR News, I'm Tony Gonzalez in Nashville.
- The FBI says it foiled a plot to attack
Minnesota's Mall of America.
The bureau says it has arrested an 18-year-old
who had been under investigation for nearly two years.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio has delivered a speech
in Athens, Greece that was filled
with Christian nationalist rhetoric,
and piers Michelle Kellerman has more.
- With the Acropolis as a backdrop,
Secretary Rubio says the world has much to learn
from the men of ancient Greece,
who knew there was nothing selfish
about fighting for their own interests.
But he says nationalism has become a dirty word,
and now the West is at a crossroads.
- The course we take will determine
whether the West maintains its place
at the head of the world or resigns itself
to a future of atrophy and servitude and decline.
- Rubio says the Trump administration plans
to dominate the fields of drone warfare,
critical minerals, and artificial intelligence,
which Trump is trying to rebrand as superintelligence
to play down calls for regulations.
Michelle Kellerman, NPR News, the State Department.
- President Trump says he is turning
part of a private golf club he owns in Florida
into a presidential-style retreat like Camp David.
More from NPR's Emily Fang.
- Representatives from the West Palm Beach Golf Club

Future presidents, according to these plans,

Trump says the golf club would be safer.
- You don't have high buildings looming over it.
There's no high building looming over it,
which is no good either.
And they can get maximum safety.
It's a great idea.
- He's also touted safety as one of the primary reasons
for building the East Wing Ballroom at the White House
and building a massive new triumphal arch in Washington.
Emily Fang, NPR News, the White House.
- You're listening to NPR News.
U.S. Gulf Coast communities are preparing
for what could be the first hurricane of the Atlantic season.
Tropical storm East I.E. has formed today
on the warm waters off eastern Mexico.
It is projected to quickly gain strength
and make landfall as soon as Friday night.
Gulf oil production's been suspended.
In Alabama, the National Shrimp Festival
that attracted over 300,000 people last year is canceled.
And Florida has declared a state of emergency
for 25 counties in the Panhandle and Big Ben regions.
The gut microbiome plays a key role
in keeping us healthy.
A new study finds that modern indigenous populations
share many ancient microbes
that most of the world is missing,
and PR's Ping Wong has details.
- The Hadza people of Tanzania
and the Chamani people of Bolivia
lived thousands of miles in an ocean apart.
Yet researchers compared their gut bacteria
and found they had 90% of the same species
in their digestive tracts.
Justin Sonnenberg at Stanford University
is senior author on the paper.
- These populations in South America and in Africa
and probably in other parts of the world
are transmitting microbes over generations.
- The similarities in their gut bacteria are remarkable.
Sonnenberg and his colleagues found that most
of these bacteria are missing
in modern industrialized people,
which raises questions like whether losing
these microbial species could affect susceptibility
to chronic and inflammatory diseases
such as certain cancers or diabetes.
The paper is published in the journal "Nature."
Ping Wong, NPR News.
- I'm Lakshmi Singh, NPR News.
